articleTitle: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
summary: The review describes Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro as a $1,999 laptop that improves performance while retaining the design Apple has used since 2021, without the OLED touchscreen and other changes featured in higher-end models. Its mini LED display, additional ports, and active cooling remain advantages over the MacBook Air, but the reviewer questions its value, especially for buyers who do not need the mandatory 1TB storage allotment.

coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The reviewer argues that a $1,999 entry-level MacBook Pro no longer provides Apple's best screen or latest design, while its mandatory 1TB storage allotment and questionable $500 to $700 upgrade value over the MacBook Air make its positioning awkward.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: No regulatory precedent is discussed. Historical examples include the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros retaining Apple's 2016-era design and Touch Bar, and the entry-level tier not receiving the 2021-era design until the M3 version was released in 2023.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The $1,999 starting price does not include the optional $150 nano-texture matte display upgrade.
The 1TB storage allotment is mandatory even for buyers who do not need it.
RAM starts at 16GB, with only 24GB and 32GB upgrade options stated; the reviewer identifies RAM as the biggest limitation for the kinds of models that run well on an M6.
The 16GB configuration is limited to 153 GB/s memory bandwidth; 24GB and 32GB configurations receive 170 GB/s.
The review unit has 16GB of RAM, versus 24GB in the comparison M6 Mac mini, and the reviewer reports 90 percent of that Mac mini's memory bandwidth.
The retained 2021 design lacks the OLED touchscreen, Dynamic Island, half-pound weight reduction, and glowing Apple logo described for newer higher-end models.
The M6 offers better single-core CPU performance and a larger Neural Engine, but the M5 Pro's higher core count wins decisively in multi-threaded CPU work.
The reviewer expects gains over M4 or M5 systems to be noticeable but not staggeringly large.
The expectation that the MacBook Air will receive M6 is not a confirmed announcement in the article.
The suggestion that M6 will not receive Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations is explicitly presented as a rumor.
The possible wait of at least two years for an OLED touchscreen is the reviewer's speculation, not an Apple commitment.
The reviewer cites ongoing RAM and storage shortages as a reason normal technology progression is uncertain.

avoidAdvice: The reviewer questions the value for buyers seeking Apple's best-possible screen or the newer flagship design: this $1,999 model lacks OLED and touch.
The reviewer questions paying for the mandatory 1TB storage allotment when it is unnecessary, particularly given the stated $500 to $700 upgrade value comparison with the MacBook Air.
For existing M4 or M5 users, the review describes the performance improvement as unlikely to feel staggeringly large.
fitAdvice: Buyers seeking the cheapest Apple laptop route to a 120 Hz ProMotion display or the optional $150 nano-texture finish.
Buyers who value the additional ports and reduced need for dongles compared with the MacBook Air.
Users with sustained workloads who benefit from active cooling rather than the MacBook Air's fanless design.
Existing M1 or M2 MacBook Air or Pro users, whom the reviewer says should notice a sizable upgrade in day-to-day use.
